title: SpaceX Sued by 2 States Over Grok’s Sexualized Images of Women and Children
snippet: People used Grok to generate millions of “spicy mode” images.
fullText:
Oregon and Virginia on Monday filed lawsuits against SpaceX, alleging that Elon Musk’s company violated consumer protection laws, months after people used Grok Imagine to generate millions of sexualized images of women and children.

Grok Imagine is an image- and video-generation tool developed by SpaceXSI, a division of SpaceX. Shortly after launching last summer, the tool added a “spicy mode,” which enabled people to generate images and videos showing partial nudity and adult-themed videos. Grok Imagine is integrated into Grok, which is Musk’s AI chatbot.

In the lawsuits, separate but jointly filed, Virginia and Oregon allege that the sexualized images — including child sexual abuse material — were generated without the knowledge and consent of the women and children shown in the images and videos.

			

More from CNET

Read more: After Rampant AI-Powered Abuse, Grok Doubles Down

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in a press release that SpaceX misled people into thinking that their images and data would be safe.

“When xAI [now renamed SpaceXSI] allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

Donna Rice Hughes, CEO of child internet safety organization Enough Is Enough, praised Oregon and Virginia for taking action against SpaceX.

“It is abhorrent that women and children are preyed upon in this manner and even more repugnant that xAI’s Grok ‘spicy mode’ has not kept up with bad actors who abuse their terms of service,” Hughes told CNET, adding that Musk’s “team can find ways to prevent criminal misuse of Grok, and at the very least, disable Grok’s ‘spicy mode.'”

What happened with Grok?

Grok Imagine launched on Aug. 5, 2025, and within months, it was used to generate millions of sexualized images, which were posted on the social media platform X, which is also owned by Musk’s SpaceX.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield alleged SpaceX “knowingly designed” Grok Imagine and promoted spicy mode’s lack of safeguards as a feature, not a bug.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material,” Rayfield said in a statement. “The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”

During a 9-day span starting in late December, Grok posted about 3 million sexualized images, according to an analysis from the Center for Countering Digital Hate.

In a statement posted Monday on X, SpaceX said that people using Grok to generate sexualized images and videos violated the platform’s terms of service and worked “aggressively to circumvent our safeguards.” The company said it tightened protections after the misuse and continues to test and adjust them as needed. SpaceX also said it notifies law enforcement authorities “when someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content.”

Grok has been sued before

Earlier this year, several minor Jane Does filed a proposed class action lawsuit against xAI after people used their photos to generate child sexual abuse material using Grok via spicy mode. That case is still ongoing.

In July, a victim’s family also filed suit after photographer Russell Bloodworth in Arkansas allegedly used spicy mode to generate explicit photos of children. xAI went on the offensive, suing Bloodworth and South Carolina man Terry Wayne Harwood, who is also accused of using Grok to generate child sexual abuse material. The company seeks damages for expenses incurred in fighting lawsuits and for reputational harm.

SpaceX and xAI have faced lawsuits for other things aside from illicit image generation. The companies were sued for allegedly sharing sensitive data and for allegedly causing users to be hospitalized for psychosis after harmful chat conversations on Grok.

Monday’s lawsuits against SpaceX are among nearly 400 cases brought against 129 AI companies in the US, according to the AI Lawsuit Tracker. Many Big Tech companies have been sued for allegedly harming the mental health of adults and children. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a lawsuit brought by US states alleging the company intentionally designed Instagram and other platforms to be addictive to children.

Companies such as ByteDance — owner of TikTok — Snap, Google and others face more than 2,400 federal lawsuits alleging that their platforms harm the mental health of children.

title: iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when new iPhone features are coming
snippet: iOS 27.3 is coming soon, packed with new features for iPhone users. Here’s when to expect the next big iPhone software update. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.3 is coming soon, packed with new features for iPhone users. Here’s when to expect the next big iPhone software update.

iOS 27.3 confirmed to launch in December, likely by mid-month

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched late last month around the same time as releases in years past. The only difference is that normally iOS 27.1 would launch in late October rather than 27.2. But since Apple made iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

Apple has confirmed that iOS 27.3 will launch to all users in December once beta testing concludes.

To get more precise though, here’s a sampling of release patterns for comparable x.2 updates the last few years:

iOS 26.2: Friday, December 12

iOS 18.2: Wednesday, December 11

iOS 17.2: Monday, December 11

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release by mid-December.

title: YouTube appears to be quietly testing a new mute button in its video UI
snippet: Users are seeing the option to mute a video appear in the YouTube app on Android, but it isn’t showing up for everyone. more…
fullText:
Users are seeing the option to mute a video appear in the YouTube app on Android, but it isn’t showing up for everyone.

Screenshots of a new video control button have started appearing on Reddit over the last week. The posts haven’t exactly begun hot debates, but it’s an interesting UI change. A mute button now sits next to the fullscreen option in the left section of the video player. Tapping it does nothing other than cut audio, until it’s tapped again to unmute.

One user details the app version on their Pixel 11 Pro XL – version 21.46.522. They also note that other devices they’ve checked on the YouTube app versions don’t appear to show any sort of mute button in the UI. Without many comments on either post, it’s hard to nail down just how wide this rollout might be.

In reality, this seems like a very small UI design test for the YouTube app. YouTube will often select a small number of users to push experimental features to while they polish them further before release. Unlike features that Premium users get to test, these are locked.

	

It’s not necessarily a big change, but it’s sort of a confusing one. One wonders why a mute button is necessary. It also adds another button to accidentally hit when trying to tap the fullscreen option.

What do you think? If you’re seeing a mute button in the YouTube app, let us know your thoughts and what kind of phone you’re using.

title: WhatsApp testing stickers with audio, including make-your-own option
snippet: WhatsApp is currently testing a new sticker format that plays a sound when the recipient taps on it. You can choose from a range of standard stickers as well as create your own by converting a video … more…
fullText:
WhatsApp is currently testing a new sticker format that plays a sound when the recipient taps on it. You can choose from a range of standard stickers as well as create your own by converting a video … 

The feature was spotted by WABetaInfo in the beta version of the Android app. 

WhatsApp is developing a new format to add an audio track to a sticker. This would allow users to send a sticker that plays a sound when the recipient taps it. 

You can create your own audio stickers by selecting one of your videos.

Once users choose a video from their gallery, WhatsApp converts it into an animated sticker automatically. At the top of the editor, users can find a new audio button that lets them add a sound to the sticker. If users tap this button, WhatsApp will display a new “Add sound” screen. This section lets users refine the new sound sticker by choosing which audio track to attach to it.

Sounds don’t play automatically, but recipients will see a small audio icon attached to the sticker, and tapping it will play the sound.

As usual with WhatsApp, it’s rolling out first in the Android beta and is likely to reach the iPhone sometime later. This can range from a few weeks to a few months, depending on how well the beta test goes.

Screen size is only one part of the whole story. The Galaxy Tab S11, S12+, and S12 Ultra have AMOLED displays that offer rich contrast for movies and photos, while the FE models provide useful everyday features at a more accessible price.

Who should buy the Galaxy Tab S12+?

The Galaxy Tab S12+ is the sweet spot if you want a serious upgrade over a basic tablet without moving to Samsung’s biggest screen.

As we covered in our Galaxy Tab S12 launch story, it combines a 12.6-inch 120Hz AMOLED display with a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen, with four months of complimentary Adobe Photoshop access and a six-month Notability trial, both of which support the stylus.

The S12+ is easy to use and appreciate in daily life. It puts reference material beside your notes during a course, sketch ideas for a presentation, while making it easy to settle into a movie after finishing your email. It has room to spread out without requiring the Ultra’s larger footprint.

The Galaxy Tab S12+ also offers a 5G version, making it worth considering if you regularly work away from Wi-Fi.

When is the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra worth it?

Buy the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra when the screen itself is the upgrade you’ll enjoy every day.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is made for creative professionals and families seeking premium entertainment. It moves naturally between focused creative work and immersive movie nights at home.

Its 14.6-inch AMOLED display gives photos, drawings, and multiple app windows more breathing room. Picture reviewing a document while keeping your handwritten notes visible, or drawing with reference images alongside your canvas.

The Ultra shares the S12+’s Dimensity 9500 processor but offers configurations up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. It’s available for $1,399.99, but last year’s Tab S11 Ultra is on sale during Black Friday for just $899.99.

Both S12 tablets ship with Android 17-based One UI 9 and seven years of OS and security updates. Photoshop comes pre-installed with a four-month access offer, giving you a way to explore S Pen-assisted photo editing.

The Ultra is especially appealing with a keyboard at a desk; Samsung’s Ultra Book Cover Keyboard Slim is the perfect companion to the S12 Ultra, and is on sale for $146.99 during Best Buy’s Black Friday Deal event.

Is the Galaxy Tab S11 still a good buy?

Yes, the Galaxy Tab S11 is the premium Galaxy tablet to choose when portability comes first.

Our Galaxy Tab S11 launch coverage highlighted the return of Samsung’s smaller flagship tablet, with a Dimensity 9400+ processor, 12GB of RAM, and an included S Pen. Its 11-inch AMOLED screen makes it an attractive companion for reading, travel, and handwritten notes.

The Galaxy Tab S11 is the sort of tablet you can bring to a meeting or pull out on a train without needing a large work surface. You still get premium display quality, just in a size that’s easier to carry, and it comes in at a lower price.

A discounted Tab S11 Ultra can also be worth considering if you want a 14.6-inch screen. Compare the actual price with the S12 Ultra rather than dismissing an older flagship automatically.

Which Galaxy Tab offers the best everyday value?

The Galaxy Tab S10 FE and FE+ are compelling choices for people who want an included S Pen without flagship pricing.

Choose the 10.9-inch FE for a study companion that travels easily. Choose the 13.1-inch FE+ when you’d rather put a lecture, document, or recipe beside your notes. Both offer IP68 water and dust resistance, so they’re great kitchen companions.

Galaxy Tab S10 Lite is for students, children, and emerging creators. It is a practical, encouraging gift for handwritten learning, organization, drawing, and experimentation.

The Galaxy Tab A11+ is the straightforward entertainment choice. At $199, it’s the cheapest of the Galaxy Tab options, but it doesn’t support the S Pen, so choose an S-series model if handwriting matters.

Which Galaxy Tab is right for you?

Choose the Galaxy Tab S12+ for a premium all-rounder, the S12 Ultra for a spacious creative workspace, or the S11 for flagship features in a travel-friendly size.

For school, home projects, and everyday notes, the FE series delivers the features many people actually need. For family streaming and browsing, the A11+ keeps things simple and affordable.

The best Galaxy Tab isn’t automatically the biggest or newest. It’s the one that makes the things you already love doing easier — and gives you a few new possibilities along the way.

title: Google Maps update on Android Auto adds navigation routes for motorcycles
snippet: Google Maps is rolling out an update on Android Auto that provides better navigation routes specifically for motorcycles. more…
fullText:
Google Maps is rolling out an update on Android Auto that provides better navigation routes specifically for motorcycles.

Users in India have recently noticed that Google Maps for Android Auto is showing a new message asking them to restart the app to “switch to two-wheeler directions.” Once enabled, a motorcycle icon appears on the ETA card.

On a support page, Google details this mode, explaining that the mode tailors directions to skip routes where two-wheelers are not allowed, while also included narrow roads that may be faster. Google says that the feature is only available in “limited locations.”

These directions show you routes away from roads where two-wheelers aren’t allowed. You may be directed towards shortcuts along narrower side roads.

The page also explains that it is only available for mobile devices, with no mention of Android Auto and CarPlay. Yet, a number of users are seeing the adjustment on their devices within the past two weeks, so it seems Google is expanding it out to Android Auto. That makes sense, as Android Auto has been working to better accommodate motorcycles for a while, and some motorcycles even now have Android Auto support built-in.

title: I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls
snippet: Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed. more…
fullText:
Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

	

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

title: Kodak SlideTag is a $35 Android & iPhone tracker with an E-Ink display to show your photos and more [Gallery]
snippet: AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s new SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items. more…
fullText:
AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s new SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items.

Compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same company that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera. 

SlideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only shows up in one out of every 64 boxes. 

The E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS. 

	

Connect instantly via Bluetooth to the KODAK Memory Link App. From live slideshows and custom QR codes to countdowns and dual-network tracking with Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub, the KODAK SlideTag seamlessly integrates retro aesthetics into your everyday carry.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

fullText:
Still waiting for tech like the Vision Pro, but in normal everyday glasses and sunglasses? The industry leader in AR glasses shipments has something to say.

The best Apple accessories share a distinct DNA: immaculate industrial design, lightweight ergonomics, tactile physical precision, and friction-free performance that feels native from minute one. Launched globally this fall, the RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo iO pair premium materials and bleeding-edge optics with the one thing Mac and iPhone owners actually want from a display accessory — plug it in, and it works.

RayNeo isn’t a small player making a big claim here. The company took the No. 1 spot in global AR smart glasses shipments across the first half of 2026, with 24.8% market share according to IDC and 23.9% according to Counterpoint Research.

Its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is live now through November 30, with the flagship GT Max at $335 (down from $429), the lighter GT at $249 (down from $329), and the camera-free iO smart glasses at $389 (down from $499). Everything is available on RayNeo.com and Amazon US.

Turn your iPhone into a 307-inch screen with RayNeo GT Max — no headset required

Watching a movie on your iPhone is convenient, but craning your neck for a comfortable view is hardly cinematic. Having a premium AR display in sunglasses form, without packing a bulky mixed-reality headset or computing puck, opens up entirely new possibilities.

The RayNeo GT Max and RayNeo GT connect to your device over a single USB-C cable. Instead of clunky goggles, the GT Series puts a massive virtual display — 59 degrees of field of view on GT Max, to be exact — into a sleek, understated sunglasses design that blends into coffee shops and airport lounges at just 68 to 78 grams. That single USB-C connection carries uncompressed video and powers the glasses directly: no secondary battery packs to carry, no charging anxiety, and zero wireless lag.

One thing to check before you buy: the glasses need a device that outputs video over USB-C (DisplayPort Alt Mode). That covers the iPhone 15, 16 and 17 series, Macs from 2015 onward with USB-C, iPad from the 10th generation on, and USB-C handhelds like the Steam Deck. The iPhone 16e, 17e and iPhone Air have USB-C ports but don’t output video over them, so they aren’t supported. Consoles and older Lightning devices need RayNeo’s HDMI adapter.

Both GT Max and GT use dual 1080p Micro-OLED panels, delivering a Full HD image to each eye with ultra-smooth 120Hz refresh rates in 2D mode. GT Max adds 38 pixels per degree, 98% DCI-P3 cinematic color coverage, and TÜV Rheinland triple eye-comfort certification. Each model offers three selectable virtual screen sizes, depending on how immersed you want to be:

GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

A private external display that travels with your Mac

The GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Both GT and GT Max include three native 3DoF hardware display modes, meaning you can position your virtual screen around your head:

Follow keeps the display centered smoothly in front of you as you turn your head.

Pinned locks your virtual display in place in 3D space, letting you glance naturally between your MacBook keyboard and your floating multi-window setup.

Steady dampens micro-movements to keep the screen rock-solid on turbulent flights.

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. The glasses draw minimal power directly from the connected device and include a four-speaker spatial acoustic array co-tuned by Bang & Olufsen, with a directional Whisper Mode that cuts sound leakage on a plane or in an office. 

GT Max also comes in three sizes based on inter-pupillary distance (IPD) — small for under 64mm, medium for 64–67mm, large for over 67mm — ensuring a tailored, comfortable fit.

Keep speaking notes, live translations, and AI tools in view with RayNeo iO

If an everyday display frame came out of Cupertino today, it would look like RayNeo iO. Rather than heavy visors, iO pairs with your iPhone through the RayNeo app to project glanceable, contextual intelligence into genuine everyday eyewear.

iO uses a high-efficiency binocular MicroLED optical engine to float high-contrast green text into your sightline, presenting a virtual image equivalent to a 33-inch screen viewed from two meters away. With peak eye-level brightness rated at 1,300 nits, reading notes and prompts stays crystal clear even under direct midday sun without occluding your real-world surroundings. The waveguide is 97% transparent and the optical engine is hidden inside the frame, so from the outside these read as ordinary glasses — most people never clock them as smart eyewear at all.

For presentations and pitches, the built-in teleprompter scrolls your notes in sync with your natural speaking cadence, so you keep your eyes locked on your audience instead of looking down at your phone. During face-to-face meetings or international travel, the glasses deliver live subtitles and two-way translation right on the lenses, with support for 55 languages and 109 accents at roughly one second of latency.

Turn-by-turn navigation and an evolving suite of OTA features

Beyond live translation and teleprompting, RayNeo iO acts as a constantly evolving heads-up companion. RayNeo pushes frequent over-the-air (OTA) software updates, continually expanding what the glasses can do throughout your day.

Just now coming to iO is heads-up turn-by-turn navigation, which projects glanceable directional arrows, street names, and real-time transit alerts directly into your line of sight. Whether you’re walking through a new city or cycling down busy streets, you can navigate without holding your iPhone in front of you or looking down at your wrist. Alongside navigation, regular software updates continue to introduce new lifestyle tools, customizable notification filters, and contextual dashboard widgets that keep the hardware feeling fresh.

There’s more coming in December, too: RayNeo is opening the iO SDK to the public, so third-party apps — and community-built ones from people with no development background — start landing on the platform shortly after the holidays.

Capture meeting notes and follow-ups without cameras

RayNeo iO’s productivity tools extend that concept further with a focus on personal privacy. This is where they really shine in the Apple ecosystem. Skipping camera modules entirely, the glasses eliminate the social friction of camera-equipped smart eyewear, making them far easier to wear into a boardroom or a client meeting.

A four-microphone array with a bone-conduction sensor captures clear audio for automated meeting minutes and AI summaries that extract key action items. RayNeo V1 and Google Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite are built in and free out of the box — no subscription required for everyday voice response, contextual reasoning, and ambient assistance. On the temple, an intuitive Smart Crown lets you scroll notifications and highlight key moments with familiar, physical micro-precision.

The titanium frames weigh just 33 grams and are rated IP54 for dust and water resistance, with a battery good for up to two days of typical use, 6.2 hours of continuous live translation, and a 25-minute charge to 80%.

iO supports Bluetooth 5.4 and carries Apple’s MFi (Made for iPhone) certification. It also has no speakers by design — which sounds like an omission until you realize what it buys you. RayNeo’s ultra-slim titanium temple arms sit flush against your ears and leave them completely free, so your AirPods stay in with Spatial Audio, Transparency Mode, and Active Noise Cancellation untouched for music and calls, while iO handles your heads-up visual intelligence.

Save on RayNeo smart glasses for Black Friday and Cyber Monday

RayNeo’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run November 19 through November 30 on RayNeo.com and Amazon US, in two phases: the main Black Friday sale through November 26, then Black Friday Weekend and Cyber Monday from November 27 to November 30.

RayNeo iO is $389, down from $499 (22% off), and the bundle with the portable eyewear charging case is $428, down from $549. Two extras make the iO deal considerably better than the sticker suggests:

title: Google Health 5.13 rolling out: Improved food search, more swimming controls
snippet: Version 5.13 of Google Health is rolling out to Android and iOS with updates across five areas. It’s a modest release that reiterates recent launches. more…
fullText:
Version 5.13 of Google Health is rolling out to Android and iOS with updates across five areas. It’s a modest release that reiterates recent launches.

Google is highlighting the availability of step-by-step workouts on the Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop. It rolled out with an update to the on-watch Google Health app, while we wait for Wear OS 7.1 to bring the other additions.

There’s also a reminder that apps and clocks are going away on older Fitbit OS smartwatches.

Activity and Fitness Updates

	

In-Progress Automatic Activity Detection: If you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

More Controls for Swimmers: You can now set your default pool length and unit preferences (meters or yards) for your swims for improved distance tracking. Go to your profile, then Google Health settings, and then Activity preferences to change your settings.

Step by Step Workouts: If you use Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5, you can now get live step-by-step guidance on your watch during each exercise in your workout.  Learn more.

Nutrition Updates

Food search has been improved to help you more easily locate items.

More Options for Settings

You can now select ‘Prefer not to say’ or ‘An option not listed’ when selecting your sex during Google Health onboarding. If you select one of these options, you’ll then be asked to choose whether you’d like your metrics to be calculated based on studies of cisgender men or studies of cisgender women.

If your preferences change, you can find these settings at any time in the Health tab by scrolling to Personal info, tapping Profile, and editing your Sex settings.

Apple Health Sync Updates

We’ve fixed an issue that affected a small number of users after the daylight saving time change where Google Health stopped sending some data to Apple Health. Syncing will resume after this fix.  If you were impacted and still have gaps in your Apple Health data, sign out of the Google Health app and sign back in to send any missing data to Apple Health.

Apps and Clocks on Fitbit Smartwatches

Starting on November 28, 2026, you can no longer install or update third-party apps and clocks on Fitbit smartwatches.

After this date, your installed apps and clock faces from third-party developers will continue to work. However, if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.

You will continue to have access to a diverse gallery of apps and clocks developed by Fitbit and Google.

This change impacts users of Fitbit Sense, Fitbit Sense 2, Fitbit Versa 4, Fitbit Versa 3, Fitbit Versa 2, Fitbit Versa Lite, and Fitbit Versa.

title: Which Samsung folding phone is right for you? Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ultra, or Flip 8
snippet: Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season. more…
fullText:
Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 vs Fold 8 Ultra vs Flip 8: What you need to know

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:

	

Galaxy Z Fold 8

Displays: 5.5-inch outer, 7.6-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 9.7mm when folded

Weight: 201 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 1TB/16GB

Cameras: 50MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP selfie (one on each display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 4,800 mAh

Charging: 45W wired, 20W wireless

Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra

Displays: 6.5-inch outer, 8-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 8.9mm when folded

Weight: 215 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 1TB/16GB

Cameras: 200MP main, 50MP ultrawide, 10MP 3x telephoto, 10MP selfie (one on each display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 5,000 mAh

Charging: 45W wired, 20W wireless

Galaxy Z Flip 8

Displays: 4.1-inch outer, 6.9-inch inner, both up to 120Hz

Thickness: 13.1mm when folded

Weight: 180 grams

Chip: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy

Storage/RAM: Up to 512GB/12GB

Cameras: 50MP main, 12MP ultrawide, 10MP selfie (on inner display)

OS: One UI 9 based on Android 17

Battery: 4,300 mAh

Charging: 25W wired, 15W wireless

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

What Samsung foldable has the best cameras?

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. 

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras. 

What Samsung foldable has the best battery life?

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life. 

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

Why buy a folding phone in the first place?

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more. 

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra. 

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

Can I transfer everything from my old phone?

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

Where to buy a Samsung foldable

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

title: AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade
snippet: AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade. more…
fullText:
AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

#1: Precision Finding works from much greater distances

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

#2: Significantly louder built-in speaker

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

fullText:
Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a new option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting.

The last major change to Google Maps styling came in 2023 (yes, time flies) when the platform rolled out a new color palette to all users. This was divisive among users, but ultimately worked out. 

Now, Google appears to be working on another new shake-up.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted a new “high-visibility” toggle in the latest Google Maps update for Android, with the new style having darker colors for the map in both light and dark modes, as well as a purple line for your route compared to the blue we’re used to seeing. 

	

Standard
High-visibility
Standard
High-visibility

The change was also spotted on Android Auto, with much darker colors (including a near-black dark mode) in both color settings for your car’s display. This is likely tied to this new “High-visibility” setting, but it’s hard to say for certain – teardowns and enabling new features early can only tell us so much.

This appears to all be controlled by a new “Map style” setting in Google Maps, with “Standard” and “High-visibility” settings available. Functionally, everything remains the same, it’s just a new set of colors. 

So, where the previous color changes were forced on all users, this one is at least optional, and the “High-visibility” naming seems like it’s targeted at those with difficulties in sight more so than just a general change for all users.

title: Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 vs Watch 9: When is it right to spend more?
snippet: The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch. Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. fullText:
The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

What do the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and Watch 9 have in common?

As we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

	

That shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

How do their specifications compare?

The clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size. 

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

The Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

How would you use these watches in everyday life?

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:

A busy workweek: The Watch 9 handles everyday activity and sleep tracking without the Ultra’s larger footprint. Its lighter case is especially appealing if you want to wear your watch through meetings, workouts, and bedtime.

A weekend on the trails: The Ultra 2 lets you follow a prepared route and check elevation as the climb gets steeper. Its brighter display makes a quick glance more useful when you’d rather keep moving than shade the screen.

Training for a race: Both offer Daily Cardio Load, so recovery guidance isn’t reserved for the expensive model. Choose the Ultra 2 when trail-specific tools and extra battery headroom also fit your training.

A trip with full days out: The Ultra 2’s longer rated endurance offers more flexibility between charges. The Watch 9’s smaller design may be more appealing if you prioritize comfortable overnight wear and can charge during your daily routine.

Which Galaxy Watch should you buy?

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

If you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling new generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

title: YouTube’s iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app launched on the platform. 

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design. 

	

Users would be able to change the app icon via a new setting in the app near the “Appearance” section, but nothing is live just yet. We also don’t know if this is Android-only, if this is limited to Premium subscribers, or when this might debut.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

title: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brought new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it includes key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

Upgraded search

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

From Apple’s website:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my usage, iOS 27 has fixed that.

New suggestions that include third-party apps

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they have a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply improvements

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple says that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Siri AI capabilities

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

Bug fixes

Beyond new features, Apple also says that iOS 27 makes the Mail app run better than ever thanks to bug fixes and performance improvements. Here are some specific examples given:

Faster message loading in Mail

More reliable search indexing in Mail

Improved list formatting in Mail

Improved unread badge accuracy in Mail

title: OnePlus starts shutting down its website to ‘focus on customer support’
snippet: After shutting down its US operations earlier this year, OnePlus has quietly closed its website in some regions as it shifts to “focus on customer support.” more…
fullText:
After shutting down its US operations earlier this year, OnePlus has quietly closed its website in some regions as it shifts to “focus on customer support.”

OnePlus announced in July that it would end new product launches in the US and Europe. Just weeks later, the OnePlus 15 and other products the brand was selling in the US were sold out for good and, more recently, OnePlus rolled out its Android 17 update to transition devices to Oppo’s ColorOS instead of OxygenOS.

Now, OnePlus has fully pulled the plug on its US website, as well as some other regions.

oneplus.com/us has purged all product listings, including for accessories, with a new message saying that the brand is “streamlining” the site:

	

Following our July 16, 2026 announcement, OnePlus is streamlining this website to focus on customer support for existing OnePlus devices. For warranty, repair, and other support, please visit our support site Click.

The same applies to the OnePlus website in the Canada, and other regions, though the UK and EU countries such as France still have an operational site that mostly push Oppo products over remaining OnePlus devices, a practice that started a few months ago prior to the shutdown. The OnePlus 15, for example, is no longer available to purchase in the UK at all. Presumably, though, the OnePlus website will shut down in these regions eventually as well. 

The OnePlus website in India is unaffected and still selling devices.

The warranty website OnePlus links to appears to be more than a bit out of date, with a focus on 2023’s OnePlus Open. The most recent device mentioned is the OnePlus 13, though the page has been updated based on what we’re able to see on the Wayback Machine.

RIP OnePlus.

by  Andrew Liszewski

Nov 26, 2026, 4:38 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

US District Judge Loren AliKhan has blocked the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses in a preliminary injunction, and rejected its efforts to dismiss ABC’s First Amendment lawsuit. ABC has accused the FCC of violating its free speech rights and claims the agency “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over content it broadcast. In her ruling the judge noted that the network was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim.”

Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump.

In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest.

”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

snippet: Samsung’s premium RGB LED TV has the widest color gamut I’ve measured this year. RGB LED TVs finally became affordable in 2026, and there's always a lot of promise when new TV technologies come out. fullText:
RGB LED TVs finally became affordable in 2026, and there’s always a lot of promise when new TV technologies come out. More color, higher brightness, improved performance — RGB LED TVs have a lot to prove. The Samsung R95H does a lot to deliver some of those promises. It can display more colors than other TVs I’ve seen so far this year, and the combination of light output and its matte screen makes it great for a bright room. RGB LED TVs might still be in their infancy, but the R95H is a solid TV that shows off the benefits of the new backlight tech.

Because RGB LED TVs use individual red, green, and blue LEDs for their backlight (instead of a field of white or blue LEDs), they can deliver more colors than LED TVs. The Samsung R95H is one of the best examples of this in RGB LED TVs. It can fully display all the colors used in the vast majority of movies (which use the P3 color space) as well as the few that use the wider BT.2020 color space.

8

Verge Score

$2500

The Good

Matte screen handles reflections incredibly well

Good color accuracy in Filmmaker mode

The Bad

Some color crosstalk in white text

Grayscale leans a bit cyan

No Dolby Vision support

The accuracy of those colors is also really good in HDR (it’s not quite as good in SDR, because the TV overbrightens most of them). Some earlier reviews called out mediocre color accuracy on the R95H, which I experienced with the first sample Samsung provided me in June. Samsung replaced that sample because I was worried something was wrong with it. But in Filmmaker mode with firmware version 1247 on my current 65-inch TV, I was pleasantly surprised by the R95H.

Samsung R95H specs

Display type: RGB LED

HDR formats: HDR10 Plus, HDR10, HLG

TV OS: Tizen OS

HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), up to 8 with Wireless One Connect box (sold separately)

Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Digital, Auracast, Q-Symphony

Gaming features: VRR (up to 165Hz), ALLM, Game Bar, FreeSync Premium Pro

Sizes available (inches): 65, 75, 85

Colors are wonderfully lifelike. The green of the jungles in Planet Earth II, which uses the expanded BT.2020 color gamut, is beautifully vibrant, as are the hummingbirds that populate the trees. With movies that use P3, the foliage in the demo material on the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc doesn’t have quite the same brilliance, but it still looks accurate and lifelike. Skin tones are natural. White and gray tones, like those in snow scenes, have a slight blue tint. It’s pretty minor, though.

The R95H also has a good amount of light output — a full-field white screen measured 694 nits, while specular highlights hit 2,206 nits in Filmmaker mode (the TV’s most accurate picture mode). That’s similar to the Sony Bravia 7 II but short of the Bravia 9 II by a few hundred nits, and well short of the TCL X11L. Flagship 2026 OLEDs also have brighter highlights but dimmer full white screens, as is expected from OLED panels. Black levels on the R95H are really good for an LED display. There’s a bit of blooming, but not as excessive as I’ve seen on some RGB LED TVs this year. Overall, the Samsung R95H delivers an impactful image.

The matte glare-free finish on the screen limits reflections well. I was never distracted by seeing the ceiling lights reflecting, as I can be with glossy screens. The black-level raise issue — where ambient light gets caught behind the matte coating, causing the screen to look more gray than black — is much better. With a bright room, the black level rises a small amount, but it’s not washed out, and dark images still have depth.

I had a great time gaming on it, too. Some earlier reviews noted issues with smearing, but recent firmware seems to have addressed this for the most part. While racing in F1 24 in 120Hz mode, motion was smooth. The TV struggled a bit more when I set the Xbox to 60Hz, but I still enjoyed playing.

Colors are lifelike and natural on the R95H in Filmmaker mode.

The back panel connections cutout includes four HDMI 2.1 ports, although additional can be added with a Wireless One Connect box.

One inherent issue with RGB LED TVs, though, is color crosstalk — I’ve seen it to some extent on every RGB LED TV, though it’s least apparent on the Sony Bravia 9 II. It can happen when there’s a dominant color onscreen near a lighter color, such as white text, lighter skin tones, or white clouds. The dominant color can bleed into those lighter colors, influencing their tint. This happens a bit on the Samsung R95H. It’s most noticeable with white text. I saw it with news tickers on a red background, making the text look subtly pink, and with gaming, particularly while playing No Man’s Sky. Text displayed above a large yellow hologram has a slight yellow coloration that disappears if I move my view away from the hologram. In fleeting moments, it’s not too distracting, but when the color around the text is consistent, the effect is noticeable.

Some TVs avoid this by defaulting the backlight to white and relying on the color filter, as LED TVs have for years. While doing that gets rid of any possibility of color crosstalk, it also diminishes the TV’s color brightness and wider gamut. So with RGB LED TV technology where it currently is in its development cycle, there’s going to be a tradeoff between some color crosstalk or a more limited color gamut.

The R95H still has the same limitations as all Samsung TVs. There’s no Dolby Vision support (Samsung is an original backer of HDR10 Plus and will likely never support competitor Dolby Vision). It also runs on Tizen OS, which is continually one of my least favorite interfaces. Everything is buried a click or two deeper than it should be, including input selection, which makes it cumbersome to use. The remote, rechargeable via both USB-C and the solar panels on the back, is small, and I’m not a fan of the button layout — they’re bunched together, and the volume control feels clunky to me.

The R95H has a sturdy pedestal stand.

The remote is the same that Samsung has used for a few years, and while it’s small, I find its layout is cramped.

The R95H is also still more expensive than most of its competitors. The Sony Bravia 9 II has better processing and is brighter, although it also has more blooming than the R95H. If you can fit a 75-inch in your space, the TCL X11L is significantly cheaper since it launched. I think it’s a better overall TV. Then there are the flagship OLEDs — Samsung’s S95H and the LG G6 — which are both less than or the same price as the R95H, depending on size. And OLED is still a step ahead of RGB LED in overall picture quality because of its better contrast.

There’s still room for RGB LED TVs to improve. With its wide color gamut coverage, good out-of-the-box accuracy, and excellent matte screen, the Samsung R95H is one of the better ones to come out this year. Put up against those RGB competitors, it makes a strong case. But OLEDs are still better overall performers with superior contrast, and even cheaper non-RGB LEDs can get you most of the way there for less.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

How I test TVs

I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.

For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

fullText:
Most people know not to try to pass highway patrol cars while performing a traffic break on a freeway. But on November 6th, a driverless Waymo on Interstate 280 failed that test.

Video shows the robotaxi attempting to overtake two California Highway Patrol cruisers during a traffic break, a moving violation that could get a human driver’s license suspended. For Waymo, it was the latest in a series of freeway blunders that eventually led to the California DMV last week banning its vehicles from all state interstates.

Construction zones have also posed a challenge. Between October and November 2026, the company reported a total of 11 instances in which its vehicles failed to recognize that a freeway lane was closed because of construction and drove into the restricted area anyway, according to a recently filed recall.

With all these violations piling up, Waymo decided last week to pause commercial freeway rides across all of its US markets. It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules.

For years, the autonomous vehicle industry assumed freeways would be the easy part — no jaywalkers, no unprotected left turns — while dense cities were seen as the ultimate battle. Yet Waymo has flipped that script, racking up millions of urban miles while repeatedly stumbling on the interstate.

It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules

This was neither the first time Waymo was forced to pause freeway operations nor the first time it had been caught blundering into construction sites. Earlier this year, the company temporarily halted freeway rides after its robotaxis entered active construction zones in Arizona and California. It issued a recall in June and gradually resumed freeway operations starting in late July after updating its software.

But experts note that the recall didn’t work, as evidenced by the subsequent violations.

”The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway,” says Phil Koopman, emeritus professor in electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and a researcher specializing in autonomous vehicle safety.

In an interview, Koopman says Waymo is using recalls as “Band-Aids,” which he argues doesn’t really address the root of the problem. In addition to the freeway snafus, Waymo also filed a recall related to the intersection crash where its vehicle failed to detect a police officer directing traffic. In short, the car followed the officer’s orders until passing traffic blocked its view, at which point its software lost track of the “stop” command and drove into the intersection on its own, the company said in the recall report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Waymo later updated its software across its entire fleet so the vehicles remember manual traffic signals even when an officer is temporarily blocked from view.

There have been other recalls related to Waymo passing stopped school buses and driving through flooded roadways. This has led Koopman to theorize that rather than solving the underlying perception and reasoning flaws, Waymo is using “dynamic geofencing” to route around known flood zones or using real-time GPS feeds of school buses until a car encounters an unmapped situation.

“The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway.”

— Phil Koopman, Carnegie Mellon University

“It felt to me like they were really not being able to fix these problems,” he says. “They’re putting Band-Aids on and getting on with scaling.”

In response to the California DMV order, Waymo said it’s working closely with regulators on a solution, noting that its vehicles haven’t crashed or injured anyone while driving through restricted areas on the freeway.

“Our ridehailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week,” Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas said last week. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

Since its inception, Waymo has typically avoided highways, opting instead for longer routes that stick to local roads when ferrying passengers. This has not gone unnoticed by the company’s customers, who often complain their trips can take longer because the vehicles are prohibited from using routes that travel on highways. But in late 2025, Waymo said it was ready to hit the highway.

“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master when we’re talking about full autonomy without a human driver as a backup,” Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo, said in a November 2025 briefing with reporters. “And at scale. So it took time to do it properly with a strong focus on system safety and reliability.”

“Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master.”

— Waymo Co-CEO Dmitry Dolgov

Now it seems as if Waymo may have jumped the gun. The company’s decision to pull back from the freeway, twice in one year, reflects the enormous stakes of operating driverless vehicles at high speeds. At 10 to 25 mph on a city street, applying the brakes solves almost any confusion, and crash lethality is drastically lower. At 60 or 70 mph, stopping distances stretch out, and any mistake involving a roadside worker or stranded motorist is nearly 100 percent fatal. And if the vehicle gets confused and needs to ping a remote operator for assistance, the latency of that connection and the time it takes to receive a reply becomes a major liability.

Koopman thinks that subtle edge cases — like a gap in construction cones or a cop’s hand gesture — are tripping Waymo up right after its transition to end-to-end machine learning. Unlike older modular systems where engineers could write explicit rules, statistical models struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar contexts.

“If you’ve trained on the individual elements, their combination presents a special meaning that is different than usual,” he says. “A stop sign folded out on a school bus is completely different from a stop sign on a post... Everything I’ve seen is consistent with the hypothesis that it’s having trouble with subtle contextual clues.”

For Waymo, solving for the freeway is essential if the company wants to continue expanding its service area to include popular ridehailing destinations, like airports. Waymo’s future reliability will depend on it. While safety engineers want to do the right thing, executives face massive market pressure to ship “good enough” fixes and apologize later, Koopman argues. And because traffic tickets and standard fines don’t deter well-capitalized tech giants like Alphabet, regulators need mandatory public transparency — not quiet software patches via recalls.

“If DMV gets a neutral look without political pressure, they’re going to say, ‘Fool me once, shame on you,’” Koopman says. “They can’t just accept Waymo saying, ‘Trust us, bro, we fixed it this time for sure.’”

For Waymo, it was the latest in a series of freeway blunders that eventually led to the California DMV last week banning its vehicles from all state interstates.

MacBook Neo

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (currently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo

Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

There are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

Still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

Update: It turns out that this feature is actually referenced in the User Guide for iPhone Duo. 

Apple made a bunch of changes to iOS to optimize it for the iPhone Duo’s form factor, including revamping the Lock Screen. According to a new leak today, the company has tested another change, referred to as a “complication column.” Here’s what it looks like. 

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

On the iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen right now, you can add widgets along the bottom of the interface. On the bottom right, you have two controls that default to the flashlight and camera. You can customize these and link them to other controls from Apple and third-party apps.

Cellular and Wi-Fi information is located along the top right-hand side of the iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen.

According to the spelunking account pdfu on X, Apple has tested a “complication column” that would appear along the right edge of the Lock Screen. The column has room for two widgets, filling the space between the flashlight/camera controls and the Wi-Fi and cellular status icons. These widgets are the same size as the widgets that appear along the bottom.

The “complication column” for iPhone Duo was first spotted in iOS 27.1 code, the account says. No code changes have been made since, so it’s unclear whether the feature is still in active development or Apple has scrapped it.

Here’s what it looks like: 

Apple has tested a “complication column” for iPhone Duo’s Lock Screen. It fits two circular widgets along the right edge.

Flag: SpringBoard/Ionic (disabled). First seen in iOS 27.1, with no code changes since. pic.twitter.com/orjOuvM1Xs

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 22, 2026

9to5Mac’s Take

I think this looks great. It’s fun seeing Apple try different things as it learns how to best design for the iPhone Duo’s form factor, which is so different from a traditional iPhone. I’d be especially intrigued to try this on the inner display’s Lock Screen, where there’s currently a lot of wasted space.

fullText:
Apple has quietly announced the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the company has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac … 

Seven stores in India after a lengthy battle

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the company has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

As we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the company has averaged two new stores a year.

India has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow company-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

The plan worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Beautiful wallpaper

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each new store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

To download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.
